fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "A Manuscript That Refuses to Be Filed Away", "body": "Jan Ott lays out what the Oera Linda actually is, a codex that surfaced in the 1870s from Cornelis over de Linden, a shipbuilder for the Dutch Marines who inherited it and could not read it. Ott describes pre Christian texts plus two letters of instruction, describing a Frisian culture with colonies in the Mediterranean and northwest India, with the main parts dating from the sixth century before our era through roughly three centuries after Alexander the Great. He notes the paper itself has never been properly studied, and that even a thirteenth century copy would carry original content."}, {"title": "The Language That Made Lying Difficult", "body": "Chance Garton raises the passage he finds most striking, a Tower of Babel style account in which the original humans placed here by the creator Vralda spoke one language built so that deceit was nearly impossible. Liars would stammer and stutter and be caught out, until mischievous men devised their own tongues for cunning and trickery. Ott agrees that when every word carries a dissectible meaning, as with the Dutch eerbied splitting into honor and offering, it becomes much harder to speak while thinking something else. Dylan Saccoccio calls the resulting trust a European vulnerability being exploited today."}, {"title": "Testing the Forgery Charge", "body": "Saccoccio presses Ott on authenticity, and Ott answers with accumulation rather than a single proof. He points to the Tollense Valley battlefield and the Swiss pile dwellings, details a nineteenth century forger could not have known or would have had no reason to include, and to obvious Frisian fantasies of that era, such as the village of Hindeloopen, that the book conspicuously omits. He argues no good theory exists for who could have made it or why, since there was no money in it. In 1870 the text was far harder to believe than a century of archaeology has since made it."}, {"title": "Sun Script, Monks and the Monogram of Christ", "body": "Saccoccio builds his case that the Oera Linda wheel is the source of a wider priestly alphabet. He ties the six spoked sun sign to the Chi Rho monogram, to the Buddhist dharma chakra and the Kalachakra, and argues Christiani is a Latin coinage from a corrupted Greek root, citing Archbishop Richard Trench and the scholar Michaelis on the late dating of gospel manuscripts. Ott adds his own example, the Alhambra numerals in southern Spain, which he says only make sense as a garbled reconstruction of numbers genuinely taken out of the Oera Linda wheel."}, {"title": "Freya's Folk, Folk Mothers and Minerva", "body": "Ott describes the social world of the text, a people who called themselves Freya's children, led not by a queen but by a folk mother at the main citadel, with maidens comparable to vestal virgins tending a perpetual fire, healing and giving counsel, and who could be punished severely for bad advice. Saccoccio and Ott then work through Minerva, called Nyhalennia, whose name Ott reads as one who lends new light, and who says she carries her possessions, love of wisdom, justice and freedom, in her bosom. Saccoccio contrasts the Latin spelling with the Etruscan Menrva as a dating clue."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Oera Linda translator and scholar Jan Ott joins InnerVerse for a conversation about this fascinating and suppressed ancient text. Dylan Saccoccio provides questions and observations for Jan Ott as we investigate clues about the history of our world through examining language and artifacts.
